lists.title: Hebrew A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Hebrew: pronoun gender, the zero copula in the present tense, adjective agreement, the ה־ definite article, present-tense verb agreement, negation with לא, existence with יש/אין, and possession with של.

lists.title: Hebrew A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Past and future in the pa'al pattern, prepositions that swallow their pronoun, the object marker את, counting with the right gender, possession with יש לי, plural agreement, and the first steps into pi'el and hif'il.

lists.title: Hebrew B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: The root-and-binyan system itself: pi'el and hif'il beyond the present, hitpa'el, the construct state, action nouns, real conditionals with אם, relative clauses with ש־, and comparison with יותר and הכי.

lists.title: Hebrew B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Nif'al, the pu'al and huf'al passives you meet in reading, counterfactual conditionals with אילו, time clauses built on ש־, reported speech without tense shift, and object pronouns.

lists.title: Hebrew C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register: the connectors and prepositions that mark written Hebrew, אשר beside everyday ש־, and construct chains that run three nouns deep.

lists.title: Hebrew C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: The vav-conversive as it survives in quotation and idiom, meaning shifts between binyanim that no rule predicts, and moving between registers inside a single text.

points.title: Personal pronouns and grammatical gender
points.function: Choose the right pronoun for gender and number
points.explanation: Hebrew marks grammatical gender on second- and third-person pronouns (not first person): אתה (you, masculine) vs. את (you, feminine); הוא (he/it, masculine) vs. היא (she/it, masculine). Every noun has a gender too, and its pronoun must match.

drills.hint: he — masculine pronoun, doubles as "is"
she — feminine pronoun; note טובה, the feminine form of "good"
you — masculine singular, contrasts with feminine את

points.title: No verb "to be" in the present tense
points.function: Build a sentence with no linking verb
points.explanation: Hebrew has no present-tense verb for "to be" — the subject sits directly next to its predicate: אני רעב ("I [am] hungry"), הבית גדול ("the-house [is] big"). Where English needs is/am/are, Hebrew just needs the two words side by side.

drills.hint: big — no "is" needed, just place it after the subject
good — again, no verb "to be"
small — the predicate follows the subject directly

points.title: Adjective gender agreement
points.function: Match an adjective's ending to its noun's gender
points.explanation: Hebrew adjectives agree in gender with the noun they describe. The feminine form usually adds ה־ to the masculine: טוב → טובה (good), קטן → קטנה (small). אישה טובה ("a good woman") but איש טוב ("a good man") — same word, different ending.

drills.hint: good, feminine — add ה־ to טוב
good, masculine — the base form, no ה־
small, feminine — add ה־ to קטן

points.title: The definite article ה־
points.function: Say "the" in Hebrew
points.explanation: Hebrew has no separate word for "the" — the definite article is the single letter ה attached directly to the front of the noun: בית ("a house") → הבית ("the house"). There is no word for "a/an" either — an unmarked noun is simply indefinite.

drills.hint: the house — ה־ prefixed directly onto בית
the book — ה־ prefixed onto ספר
the city — ה־ prefixed onto עיר

points.title: Present-tense verbs change with gender and number
points.function: Conjugate a present-tense verb for its subject
points.explanation: A Hebrew present-tense verb has four forms, agreeing with the subject's gender and number: הולך (he goes, masc. sg.), הולכת (she goes, fem. sg.), הולכים (they go, masc./mixed pl.), הולכות (they go, fem. pl.). The same pattern applies to most present-tense verbs, like אוכל/אוכלת/אוכלים/אוכלות ("eat").

drills.hint: goes — feminine singular, add ת to הולך
go — masculine plural, add ים
go — feminine plural, add ות

points.title: Negation with לא
points.function: Say what isn't or doesn't happen
points.explanation: To negate a present-tense sentence, put לא ("not") right before the predicate — no auxiliary verb needed: אני לא הולך ("I'm not going"), הבית לא גדול ("the house isn't big").

drills.hint: not — placed right before the verb
not — before the verb, no auxiliary needed
not — before an adjective works the same way

points.title: Existence: יש and אין
points.function: Say that something does or doesn't exist
points.explanation: יש ("there is/are") and its negative אין ("there isn't/aren't") state that something exists — combined with ל־ ("to"), the same word means someone HAS something: יש לי בית, literally "there-is to-me a-house" = "I have a house."

drills.hint: there is — states existence
there is
there isn't — the negative of יש

points.title: Possession with של
points.function: Say who something belongs to
points.explanation: של ("of / belonging to") is the easiest way to show possession for a beginner: הבית של דוד ("David's house", literally "the-house of David").

drills.translation: The house is David's / belongs to David.
drills.hint: of / belonging to
of — links the book to its owner

drills.translation: The city belongs to the family.
drills.hint: of / belonging to

points.title: Infinitives after רוצה and אפשר
points.function: Chain a second verb onto the first without conjugating it
points.explanation: The Hebrew infinitive begins with ל־: ללכת (to go), לדבר (to speak), לקרוא (to read). After רוצה ("want"), צריך ("need"), יכול ("can") and the impersonal אפשר ("it is possible"), the second verb stays in this one unchanging form — only the first verb agrees with the subject.

drills.hint: to go — the infinitive of the everyday verb for going and walking
to sit — the infinitive that follows the impersonal word for it is possible
to drink — infinitive, unchanged whoever the subject is
to speak — only the first verb agrees with we
to read — the second verb after can stays in its base form

points.title: Yes/no questions and question words
points.function: Ask a question in Hebrew
points.explanation: A yes/no question in spoken Hebrew keeps the word order of a statement — only the rising intonation changes (the particle האם belongs to formal writing). Questions that ask for information start with a question word: מה (what), מי (who), איפה (where), מתי (when), למה (why), איך (how), כמה (how much/many).

drills.hint: where — asks about place
what — asks about a thing
when — asks about time
how much — asks about quantity or price
why — asks for a reason
who — asks about a person

points.title: Past tense pa'al: the singular persons
points.function: Put a basic verb into the past for one person
points.explanation: The past tense marks its person with endings rather than prefixes. For the root כ־ת־ב in the plain pa'al pattern: כתבתי (I wrote), כתבת (you wrote — one spelling for masculine and feminine), כתב (he wrote), כתבה (she wrote). The third-person masculine form is the bare stem, which is why dictionaries list verbs under it.

drills.hint: I wrote — first person singular, the same for men and women
he studied — the bare stem, with no ending at all
she studied — feminine singular, the ending you also see on adjectives
you read — second person singular; the unvocalized spelling covers both genders

drills.translation: I heard the song on the radio.
drills.hint: I heard — first person singular past

points.title: Past tense pa'al: the plural persons
points.function: Put a basic verb into the past for several people
points.explanation: The plural past endings continue the same system: כתבנו (we wrote), כתבתם / כתבתן (you plural, masculine / feminine — speech uses the masculine form for both), and כתבו (they wrote), a single form that covers masculine and feminine alike.

drills.hint: we sat — first person plural past
they ate — one plural form serves both genders
they went — the ending is the same as for a masculine group
you read — second person plural past
we saw — first person plural of a verb whose root ends in a weak letter

points.title: Future tense pa'al
points.function: Say what will happen
points.explanation: Where the past uses endings, the future uses prefixes: א for I, ת for you and for she, י for he, נ for we. So from כ־ת־ב: אכתוב, תכתוב, יכתוב, נכתוב, and יכתבו for they. Feminine forms add a י ending in the singular (תכתבי); the old feminine plural forms have been replaced by the masculine ones in speech.

drills.translation: Tomorrow I will write a letter.
drills.hint: I will write — the א prefix marks first person singular

drills.translation: He will study Hebrew next year.
drills.hint: he will study — the י prefix marks third person masculine
we will study — the נ prefix marks first person plural
will you go — feminine singular future, with an extra ending
they will come — third person plural future

points.title: Prepositions with pronoun endings
points.function: Say to me, to him, at my place
points.explanation: A Hebrew preposition does not stand in front of a separate pronoun — it swallows it. ל־ ("to") gives לי, לך, לו, לה, לנו, להם; אצל ("at someone's place") gives אצלי, אצלך, אצלו; and על, עם, ב־ and מ־ all behave the same way. The set of endings is nearly identical from preposition to preposition, so learning one gets you most of the others.

drills.hint: to me — the little preposition for to, carrying a first person ending

drills.translation: I told her that everything is fine.
drills.hint: to her — feminine third person ending

drills.translation: We met at my place in the evening.
drills.hint: at my place — the preposition for someone's home, with a first person ending
to him — after the word for there isn't, it means he doesn't have

drills.translation: I'm waiting for you at the entrance.
drills.hint: to you — masculine singular ending

points.title: The object marker את
points.function: Mark a definite direct object
points.explanation: When the direct object is definite — a proper name, a noun carrying ה־, or a possessed noun — Hebrew puts את in front of it. The word has no English translation of its own; it simply flags "this is the object". An indefinite object takes nothing: אני רואה בית ("I see a house") beside אני רואה את הבית ("I see the house").

drills.hint: the untranslatable marker that stands before a definite object
needed here because a personal name counts as definite
flags the object; it is never translated into English
the marker required by the definite article on the next word
the object flag, used with plural definites too

points.title: Numbers and gender agreement
points.function: Count nouns with the right form of the number
points.explanation: Hebrew numbers come in two sets and must match the gender of what they count. Feminine nouns take אחת, שתיים, שלוש, ארבע, חמש; masculine nouns take אחד, שניים, שלושה, ארבעה, חמישה. Counterintuitively, the forms that end in ה are the masculine ones. Directly before a noun, שתיים and שניים shorten to שתי and שני.

drills.hint: three, masculine — the longer counting form
three, feminine — the short form, with no ending
four, masculine — tickets is a masculine noun
four, feminine — cakes is a feminine noun

drills.translation: There are five children in the class.
drills.hint: five, masculine
five, feminine — minutes is a feminine noun

points.title: Possession with יש ל־
points.function: Say what someone has
points.explanation: Hebrew has no verb "to have". Possession is built from יש plus ל־ with a pronoun ending: יש לי ("I have", literally "there is to me"), יש לך, יש לו, יש לה, יש לנו, יש להם. The negative swaps יש for אין: אין לי זמן. What is owned stays an ordinary indefinite noun, so it takes no object marker.

drills.hint: there is — together with the to-word it means to have
to us — first person plural ending
there isn't — the negative counterpart
to you — masculine singular

drills.translation: They have a house in Tel Aviv.
drills.hint: to them — third person plural

points.title: Noun and adjective plural agreement
points.function: Make nouns plural and keep the adjective in step
points.explanation: Masculine nouns usually take ים־ in the plural and feminine nouns ות־: ספר → ספרים, מחברת → מחברות. The adjective copies both gender and number, so the endings line up down the phrase: ספרים גדולים, מחברות גדולות. A few nouns take the "wrong" ending but keep their gender — שולחן is masculine and stays masculine as שולחנות, so it needs a masculine adjective.

drills.hint: big — masculine plural, matching the noun's ending
big — feminine plural
small — feminine plural
good — masculine plural, following its noun
big — the noun looks feminine in the plural but is masculine

points.title: Present tense pi'el
points.function: Use the second verb pattern in the present
points.explanation: Pi'el is the second big verb pattern, and its present tense is easy to spot: every form starts with מ־ and has an a-vowel in the middle — מדבר / מדברת / מדברים / מדברות (speak), מספר (tell), מבקש (ask for), מלמד (teach). Compare the plain pa'al הולך, which takes no prefix at all.

drills.translation: I speak Hebrew. (said by a man)
drills.hint: speak — masculine singular; this pattern's present begins with מ
speaks — feminine singular
talk — masculine plural
teaches — masculine singular of the same pattern
request — masculine singular

points.title: Present tense hif'il
points.function: Use the causative verb pattern in the present
points.explanation: Hif'il verbs also begin with מ־ in the present, but they carry an i-vowel before the last root letter: מרגיש (feel), מתחיל (begin), מסביר (explain), מזמין (order, invite). The other forms are regular: מרגישה, מרגישים, מרגישות. Many hif'il verbs are causative — "make someone do" — but plenty, like מרגיש, simply are what they are.

drills.hint: feel — masculine singular
feels — feminine singular
begins — masculine singular
explains — masculine singular
order — masculine plural

points.title: Roots and binyanim: how the system works
points.function: Read a verb as a root plus a pattern
points.explanation: Almost every Hebrew verb is a three-consonant root poured into one of seven patterns called binyanim, and the pattern — not the root — carries the grammatical flavour. From ל־ב־ש you get pa'al לובש ("wears"), hif'il מלביש ("dresses someone else"), and hitpa'el מתלבש ("gets dressed"). Recognizing the pattern lets you guess a new verb's meaning and conjugate it without learning it from scratch.

drills.translation: He is wearing a white shirt.
drills.hint: wears — the plain pattern of the root for clothing
dresses someone else — the causative pattern, feminine singular

drills.translation: I get dressed quickly in the morning.
drills.hint: get dressed — the reflexive pattern, masculine singular
teaches — the intensive pattern built on the root for learning
studies — the plain pattern of that same root

points.title: Pi'el in the past and the future
points.function: Conjugate a pi'el verb outside the present
points.explanation: The מ־ of the pi'el present belongs to the present only. In the past the stem takes the ordinary endings directly — דיברתי, דיברת, דיבר, דיברה, דיברנו, דיברו — and in the future it takes the ordinary prefixes: אדבר, תדבר, ידבר, נדבר, ידברו. The middle root letter is doubled in pronunciation, which is what makes the pattern sound distinct.

drills.translation: Yesterday I spoke with the manager.
drills.hint: I spoke — first person singular past of this pattern

drills.translation: He told me a long story.
drills.hint: told — third person masculine singular past

drills.translation: Tomorrow I'll speak with him about it.
drills.hint: I will speak — the future prefix for first person singular
cleaned — feminine singular past of a verb whose root ends in a weak letter

drills.translation: They told us about the trip.
drills.hint: told — third person plural past

points.title: Hif'il in the past and the future
points.function: Conjugate a hif'il verb outside the present
points.explanation: Hif'il keeps a ה־ at the front in the past: הרגשתי, הרגשת, הרגיש, הרגישה, הרגשנו, הרגישו. In the future that ה disappears and the ordinary prefixes take over: ארגיש, תרגיש, ירגיש, נרגיש, ירגישו. Notice that the long i-vowel of the present survives in the third person past and throughout the future.

drills.hint: I felt — first person singular past of this pattern
started — third person masculine singular past
you will feel — second person masculine singular future
explained — third person masculine singular past

drills.translation: They will return the money tomorrow.
drills.hint: they will give back — third person plural future

points.title: Hitpa'el: reflexive and reciprocal verbs
points.function: Say what someone does to themselves or to each other
points.explanation: Hitpa'el covers actions done to oneself or to one another. Its present adds מת־ (מתלבש, מתרחץ, מתגעגע) and its past adds הת־ (התלבשתי, התלבש, התלבשה, התלבשו). When the root begins with a hissing letter, the ת swaps places with it: השתמש ("used"), not the expected התשמש.

drills.translation: I get dressed in the morning.
drills.hint: get dressed — present, masculine singular
got dressed — past, feminine singular
miss — present, masculine singular of the same pattern
used — here the ת has swapped places with the first root letter
woke up — past, third person plural

points.title: The construct state (smichut)
points.function: Join two nouns without של
points.explanation: Instead of של, two nouns can simply be set side by side: בית ספר ("school", literally "house of book"), עוגת שוקולד ("chocolate cake"), מיץ תפוזים ("orange juice"). The first noun takes a special construct shape — feminine ה־ becomes ת (עוגה → עוגת) and masculine plural ים־ becomes י־ (ספרים → ספרי). Only the final noun may carry the definite article: בית הספר.

drills.translation: The children are going to school.
drills.hint: the book — the second half of the compound, and the only part that takes the article
cake of — the construct shape, with the feminine ending changed to ת

drills.translation: The school is on the main street.
drills.hint: house of — the first link of the compound that means school
books of — masculine plural in construct, with a shortened ending
juice — the first noun of the compound; many masculine nouns look unchanged

points.title: Verbal nouns (shem pe'ula)
points.function: Name the activity a verb describes
points.explanation: Each binyan has its own noun-of-action shape. Pa'al gives כתיבה (writing), הליכה (walking), אכילה (eating); pi'el gives דיבור (speaking) and טיול (a trip); hif'il gives הסבר (explanation) and הפסקה (a break); hitpa'el gives התלבשות. These are ordinary nouns with gender and plural, and they are the usual way to name an activity where English would use an -ing form.

drills.hint: walking, as a noun — the pa'al action-noun shape
the writing — the article plus the pa'al action noun

drills.translation: The lesson continues after a short break.
drills.hint: a break — a feminine action noun from the causative pattern

drills.translation: He gave me a good explanation.
drills.hint: explanation — the action noun of the verb meaning to make clear

drills.translation: Speaking Hebrew is hard for me.
drills.hint: speaking, as a noun — the pi'el action-noun shape

points.title: Real conditionals with אם
points.function: State a condition that may well come true
points.explanation: For a condition that could really happen, Hebrew uses אם ("if") and puts the future tense in both halves — where English keeps the present in the if-clause: אם ירד גשם, נישאר בבית ("If it rains, we'll stay home"). A command can stand in the main clause instead. For general facts the present is fine in both halves.

drills.translation: If I have time, I'll come.
drills.hint: if — introduces a condition that may genuinely happen

drills.translation: If it rains, we'll stay home.
drills.hint: we will stay — the main clause takes the future too

drills.translation: If you want, I'll help you.
drills.hint: I will help — first person singular future

drills.translation: If you're tired, go to sleep.
drills.hint: go — the masculine singular command form

drills.translation: If you don't come, we'll call you.
drills.hint: if — the ordinary word for a real condition

points.title: Relative clauses with ש־
points.function: Attach a clause to a noun
points.explanation: One prefix, ש־, does the work of who, which and that, and it glues onto the following word: האיש שגר כאן ("the man who lives here"), הספר שקראתי ("the book that I read"). Unlike English, it can never be left out. When the noun is the object of a preposition, Hebrew repeats that preposition later with a pronoun ending: הבית שגרתי בו ("the house I lived in").

drills.translation: The man who lives here is a doctor.
drills.hint: who lives — the relative prefix glued to the verb

drills.translation: The book I read was interesting.
drills.hint: that I read — the relative prefix on a past-tense verb

drills.translation: This is the restaurant we ate at yesterday.
drills.hint: that we ate — note that the preposition comes back later with an ending

drills.translation: The girl who studies Hebrew lives here.
drills.hint: who studies — feminine singular present with the relative prefix

drills.translation: This is the house I grew up in.
drills.hint: that I grew up — with the preposition echoed at the end

points.title: Comparatives with יותר and הכי
points.function: Compare two things and pick the top one
points.explanation: To compare, add יותר ("more") to the adjective and מ־ ("than") to what you compare with: דן גבוה יותר מדנה, or, just as common in speech, דן יותר גבוה מדנה. The superlative uses הכי ("most"): הוא הכי גבוה. פחות is "less", and formal writing prefers ביותר to הכי.

drills.hint: more — the word that builds the comparative

drills.translation: He is the tallest in the class.
drills.hint: most — the everyday superlative word

drills.translation: This book is more interesting than the movie.
drills.hint: more — here it comes before the adjective
more — with the prefix for than on the following word
less — the opposite of the comparative word

points.title: Nif'al: the middle and passive pattern
points.function: Use the pattern for things that happen to the subject
points.explanation: Nif'al is often the passive or middle counterpart of pa'al. Its present and past both begin with נ־ (נכנס, נפגש, נמצא; נכנסתי, נפגשנו), while the infinitive and future insert a ה: להיכנס, ייכנס. Many nif'al verbs are simply intransitive rather than passive — נגמר ("ended"), נשבר ("broke") — and the masculine singular present and past look identical.

drills.translation: We meet at the café at six.
drills.hint: meet each other — present, masculine plural
entered — masculine singular; the present and past forms are spelled alike
broke — past, feminine singular, with nobody doing the breaking
ended — masculine singular of this pattern

drills.translation: The keys are on the table.
drills.hint: are located — present, masculine plural, matching a masculine noun

points.title: Pu'al and huf'al: recognizing the passives
points.function: Read the two patterns that exist only as passives
points.explanation: Two binyanim have no active use at all. Pu'al is the passive of pi'el — present מסודר, מדובר, past סודר, בוטל ("was cancelled") — and huf'al is the passive of hif'il — present מוזמן, מוסבר, past הוזמן, הופסק. Both have a present starting with מ and an u-vowel, and neither has a subject doing the action; if the agent is named at all it arrives with על ידי.

drills.hint: was cancelled — past, feminine singular, passive of the intensive pattern
tidied — present, masculine singular of that same passive

drills.translation: I am invited to the wedding.
drills.hint: invited — present, masculine singular, passive of the causative pattern

drills.translation: The lesson was stopped halfway through.
drills.hint: was stopped — past, masculine singular of that same passive

drills.translation: The rules were explained in the lesson.
drills.hint: were explained — past, plural, passive of the causative pattern

points.title: Unreal conditionals with אילו and לו
points.function: Talk about what would happen if things were different
points.explanation: For a condition contrary to fact, אם gives way to אילו or the shorter לו, and both halves use היה plus the present participle: אילו היה לי זמן, הייתי בא ("If I had time, I would come"). The same היה + present frame also carries "used to" and polite would-statements, so context decides which reading is meant.

drills.translation: If I had time, I would come.
drills.hint: if, counterfactually — not the word used for a real condition

drills.sentence: אילו היה לי כסף, {{answer}} קונה דירה.
drills.translation: If I had money, I'd buy an apartment.
drills.hint: I was — the past of to be, which builds the conditional frame
drills.transliteration: ilu haya li kesef, ___ kone dira.

drills.translation: If I had known, I would have told you.
drills.hint: saying — the present participle after the past of to be

drills.translation: She would be glad to help.
drills.hint: she was — feminine singular of the past of to be, here with a would-meaning

drills.translation: If I were rich, I'd travel the world.
drills.hint: the shorter counterfactual conjunction, common in writing

points.title: Temporal clauses: כש־, לפני ש־, אחרי ש־
points.function: Anchor one event in time relative to another
points.explanation: Time conjunctions are built from a preposition plus ש־: כש־ ("when"), לפני ש־ ("before"), אחרי ש־ ("after"), עד ש־ ("until"), מאז ש־ ("since"). The ש appears only before a clause — before a plain noun it drops away: לפני השיעור ("before the lesson") but לפני שהשיעור מתחיל ("before the lesson starts").

drills.translation: When I got home, it was raining.
drills.hint: when I arrived — the when-prefix glued onto a past verb

drills.translation: I ate before I left the house.
drills.hint: that I went out — the linking form used after the word for before

drills.translation: After we saw the movie, we went to sleep.
drills.hint: that we saw — the linking form used after the word for after

drills.translation: We'll wait until the rain stops.
drills.hint: that it will end — the future tense after the word for until

drills.translation: When I'm tired, I drink coffee.
drills.hint: when I — the when-prefix attached straight to the pronoun

points.title: Indirect speech with ש־
points.function: Report what someone said
points.explanation: Reported speech is introduced by ש־ ("that"), and unlike English "that" it can never be dropped: הוא אמר שהוא עייף. Hebrew also does not shift the tense backwards — the reported clause keeps the tense the speaker originally used, so הוא אמר שהוא בא is "he said he was coming". A reported yes/no question uses אם ("whether").

drills.translation: He said that he was tired.
drills.hint: that he — the conjunction fused with the pronoun

drills.translation: She said she would come tomorrow.
drills.hint: that she will come — the tense stays as it was originally spoken

drills.translation: I asked whether he wanted to come.
drills.hint: whether — the same word used for a real condition
that you — the conjunction with a feminine singular pronoun
that not — the conjunction plus the negation word

points.title: Object pronouns and their literary suffixed forms
points.function: Say me, him, them as the object of a verb
points.explanation: When the direct object is a pronoun, everyday Hebrew builds it on the object marker: אותי (me), אותך (you), אותו (him/it), אותה (her), אותנו (us), אותם (them). Literary and news Hebrew can instead fuse the pronoun onto the verb itself — ראיתיו for ראיתי אותו, מצאתיה for מצאתי אותה. Those suffixed forms are worth recognizing in print, but speech uses the separate ones.

drills.translation: He saw me at the market.
drills.hint: me — the object marker carrying a first person ending
her — the object marker with a feminine third person ending
them — the plural object form

drills.translation: I saw him yesterday in town.
drills.hint: I saw him, in a single literary word — the pronoun is welded onto the verb
you — the object form of the second person

points.title: Formal and colloquial register
points.function: Choose the connector that fits the situation
points.explanation: Modern Hebrew keeps a visible gap between speech and the language of newspapers, notices and official prose. Where speech says אבל, בגלל and רק, careful writing prefers אולם or אך, בשל or מחמת, and בלבד. Formal Hebrew also keeps distinctions speech has dropped, such as the feminine plural future תלכנה. Using the high forms in casual conversation sounds as odd as the reverse.

drills.translation: The meeting was cancelled; however, the notice was sent late.
drills.hint: however — the written counterpart of the everyday word for but
only — the formal word, which follows what it limits

drills.translation: The flight was cancelled due to the weather.
drills.hint: due to — the written preposition; speech would use a different one

drills.translation: Despite the late hour, we kept working.
drills.hint: despite — used directly before a noun in careful writing

drills.translation: He did not come, although he had promised.
drills.hint: that he promised — the clause form after the formal word for although

points.title: אשר beside everyday ש־
points.function: Use the written-register relative word
points.explanation: In careful writing the relative prefix ש־ can be replaced by the free-standing word אשר, which never fuses with what follows: הדוח אשר הוגש אתמול. It is the normal choice before a preposition in formal prose — הנושא אשר עליו דיברנו — and it is frozen into set phrases such as באשר ל־. Speech uses ש־ almost exclusively, and piling up אשר sounds stilted.

drills.translation: The report submitted yesterday is very long.
drills.hint: which — the free-standing relative word of written Hebrew

drills.translation: The topic we spoke about is important.
drills.hint: which — before a preposition, formal prose prefers the separate word

drills.translation: The man who lives here is a neighbour of mine.
drills.hint: who lives — everyday speech glues the relative straight onto the verb

drills.translation: As for the budget, we'll discuss it tomorrow.
drills.hint: as for — a frozen formal phrase built on that same relative word

drills.translation: The decision taken last night was published today.
drills.hint: which — the formal relative, here inside a news sentence

points.title: Long construct chains
points.function: Read and build a chain of three or more nouns
points.explanation: A construct chain can run several nouns deep, and only the very last link may carry the definite article: משרד ראש הממשלה ("the Prime Minister's Office"), דוח ועדת החקירה. No adjective can sit inside the chain — it waits until the end and agrees with whichever noun it modifies, which is why בית הספר החדש can mean either "the new school" or, in principle, "the new book's house". Speech often breaks a long chain up with של.

drills.translation: He works in the Prime Minister's Office.
drills.hint: the government — the last link, and the only one allowed the article
house of — the first link of the compound meaning school

drills.translation: We read the report of the commission of inquiry.
drills.hint: the investigation — the final link of a three-noun chain

drills.translation: The lawyer arrived at the meeting.
drills.hint: the law — the second half of the compound that means lawyer

drills.translation: The school's pupils went on a trip.
drills.hint: the book — the closing link of a chain that begins with pupils

points.title: The vav-conversive in quotation and idiom
points.function: Recognize the biblical tense system where it survives
points.explanation: Biblical Hebrew flipped a verb's tense with a prefixed ו: ויאמר ("and he said") looks like a future but narrates the past, and והיה ("and it shall be") looks like a past but points forward. Modern Hebrew abandoned the system, yet the forms survive in quotation, liturgy, headlines and fixed idioms such as ויהי מה ("come what may"). Read them as vocabulary, not as a pattern you can extend.

drills.hint: and there was — a past narrated by a future-looking form

drills.translation: And Moses said to the people.
drills.hint: and he said — the classic narrative past with a prefixed vav

drills.translation: And it shall come to pass on that day.
drills.hint: and it will be — a past-shaped verb read as a future

drills.translation: And you shall love your neighbour as yourself.
drills.hint: and you shall love — a past form with vav read as a command

drills.translation: We'll carry on, come what may.
drills.hint: let it be — the same frozen form, here inside a modern idiom

points.title: Idiomatic shifts between binyanim
points.function: Handle roots whose meaning jumps unpredictably between patterns
points.explanation: Once a root moves between binyanim the meaning can drift in ways no rule predicts, so each pairing has to be learned as vocabulary. From ר־א־ה: ראה ("saw"), הראה ("showed"), נראה ("looked, seemed"). From ח־ז־ר: חזר ("came back"), החזיר ("gave back"), חיזר ("courted"), plus the noun חזרה ("rehearsal"). Some pairings are outright idioms: נשבר לי is literally "it broke to me" and means "I've had enough".

drills.hint: showed — the causative counterpart of the verb for seeing
look, seem — the middle-pattern form of that same root

drills.translation: I'm fed up with this job.
drills.hint: it broke — with a to-me phrase it becomes the idiom for being fed up

drills.translation: He returned the book to the library.
drills.hint: gave back — the causative of the verb for coming back

drills.translation: The actors came to the rehearsal.
drills.hint: to the rehearsal — a noun built on that same root

points.title: Switching register inside one text
points.function: Move between written and spoken Hebrew as the text demands
points.explanation: An educated writer changes register within a single paragraph, and the markers are grammatical rather than merely lexical: a formal sentence reaches for בטרם, בשל, אשר and the frame אין ב־ ... כדי, while a quoted line drops to ש־, בגלל and כי. The skill is matching the register to the moment — a news report that suddenly uses spoken connectors reads as sloppy, and a conversation full of בטרם reads as a parody.

drills.translation: Before we left, we checked the address.
drills.hint: we went out — after the elevated word for before, with no linking particle

drills.translation: That is not enough to change the decision.
drills.hint: in order to — part of a formal frame meaning is not sufficient to

drills.sentence: הוא אמר {{answer}} בא כי הוא עייף.
drills.translation: He said he wasn't coming because he was tired.
drills.hint: that not — plain spoken register, with the everyday conjunctions
drills.transliteration: hu amar ___ ba ki hu ayef.

drills.translation: The decision was taken owing to the economic situation.
drills.hint: owing to — the written causal preposition

drills.translation: We didn't come because of the rain.
drills.hint: because of — the everyday causal preposition
